title: I stopped trying to be a solo developer and started directing AI instead
author: ModernGameDev
selftext:
For a while I was stuck trying to be good at everything. Art, sound, writing, marketing. All of it.

That's the solo dev trap. You end up spending most of your time being mediocre at like 10 completely different things instead of being great at directing one vision.

Somewhere along my game dev journey I realized the job isn't "do everything yourself". It's closer to being a game director. You don't need to be the best cinematographer or the best sound designer. You just need a clear vision and the ability to get the right output from the people or tools around you.

For solo devs right now, AI is basically your crew. Concept artist, programmer, writer, even voice actor. The skill that matters most isn't mastering every department. It's knowing what quality looks like and directing toward it.

I wrote up the full medium article here if anyone wants to read the longer version: [Medium Article](https://medium.com/@themoderngamedev/why-i-stopped-being-a-solo-developer-and-became-a-game-director-cb4580f596d5)

Curious if other solo devs have felt this shift too, or if you're still in the "do it all yourself" camp.

comments.author: davesoft
comments.body: Yup, I like making games as a hobby, but there's just no time. Now I can blather my ideas at a robot and enjoy 'my own game'.

replies.author: ModernGameDev
replies.body: it **is** your game. you seeded the idea, AI only knows how to execute.

replies.author: davesoft
replies.body: I've spent the last hour indulging in 'yeah, but what if all these levels were a 3rd person shooter instead?'. That's a month of work in itself, but here I am an hour later giving it left-a-bit right-a-bit corrections. Bless the robots :D

replies.author: Coreydoesart
replies.body: This really depends. Ai gen content can’t be copywritten. So you actually can’t really own it unless you make substantial changes to the ai output. So technically and legally, most games in this sub do not belong to those who use ai to generate them.

replies.author: ModernGameDev
replies.body:
And that's what I want to teach because we all can't just accept whatever AI outputs. We have to make the changes to really make it our own. and I feel like a lot of people are just lazy and we need to get out of that mindset and start using AI as a tool to work with rather than a one-shot solution.

over time once we really understand that, we can actually make quality games and not just 'look what AI did'.

replies.author: Silencer-1995
replies.body:
The way it is for me is kinda like having the A.I teach me how to repair an engine. I have no idea what I'm doing, but I'm the one who has to crawl into all the bone and gristle and do the grunt work. Sort of the best of both worlds imo, on the one hand I'm learning as I go, but on the other hand the A.I is pushing things forwards at enough pace to keep me engaged.

I just love pottering around trying different ideas and will happily spend entire evenings just making "games" under the A.I's stewardship. All good stuff.

replies.author: davesoft
replies.body:
I'm taking more of a director role. Dev experience comes in handy with the precise language that's needed sometimes, but only about 5% of the 3d models are my work from blender, the rest is some low poly toy like meshes it's made in three.js. I've asked it if some of these can be turned into glb files and I can mess with them in blender, but I think that ruins it. Everything is either what the robot did under my instruction or something specific I make and jam in.

And of course I'm happy for this game to me For Me. Plenty of folks would decry that if it can't be monetised then why bother.. but I have a job, so I'm less doomed to seek profit.

replies.author: Silencer-1995
replies.body:
Exactly. I'm actually against commercial A.I use in gaming, because I think if we get into the world where any john, dick and harry can generate a game and sell it inside of an afternoon then... well I mean you've seen the state of Steam as it is right? And most of that is actual people doing the work. I mean if people wanna do that it is what it is, I aint going to rage out lol, but that's just my view on it.

But for personal use I think its fantastic. If vibe coding gets to a point where I can just say "Make me a ww2 themed classic resident evil clone" and it runs off and does it, I'm happy. I wouldn't want to sell it, I would just want to see my imagination unleashed and enjoy the sort of things I could only dream of as a child, silly as it sounds.

Vibe coding aint there yet from what I understand, so human monkey with A.I steward is the way I'm going until I think the A.I can do both roles effectively.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
This is going to sounds a little bit weird, and maybe I've been out of work too long, but I created chats in Codex for each role and then gave them names. Producer Paul, Architect Dave, QA Mara etc. I'm used to working with a team as a Product Owner so it's natural to direct instead of do for a lot of tasks.

It helps me to treat them as distinct personas with their own work areas and concerns. It also help them to stay within their boundaries so you don't get QA trying to implement a service architecture because it found a gap.

On top of all this I'm running a simple Kanban board so I can guide each team member where to work next and there is a common document for information to be stored. We've got a nice flow running:

My idea -> Designer planning -> Architect planning -> QA planning -> Developer planning -> Producer

Developer does the work and documents it all  
  
Architect review -> QA testing -> Designer/Me testing -> Producer closes the task and manages git.

replies.author: ModernGameDev
replies.body:
This! Thank you for sharing this is a great workflow to follow!

And I would name my chats too haha

replies.author: ScallionZestyclose16
replies.body:
If you keep reusing the same chats won’t that cause your tokens to burn out faster as the context grows as you add more files to the chat ?

Or do you have like cursor skills that you run to give them the names in a new chat prompt ?

replies.author: loontoon
replies.body:
In Claude code use /compact when your context window gets too large, use /context to check your context, use /usage to see useful stats and when you've finished a particular milestone use /clear to start a fresh context window. 

You should also be pushing everything to git and you should have told your AI to document everything in markdown files saved to your local machine as well as to git.

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
I originally started with each chat being defined and agreeing their role. Then I used the Codex tool to branch to a fresh chat for each task which maintained that base context.

TBH, that became a bit of a pain to administer and I wanted most of them to maintain some context between tasks just so they don't have to relearn everything each time. For example, the QA agent needs to remember the test harness and the quirks of the system we have accepted.

It takes a decent amount of usage with the roles split across chats to reach a state where the context needs compacting.

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
I feel this. I know AI is just a tool, but being able to be more of an ideas person and just doing the code reviews has felt like it's made all the difference.

I had so many games in various prototyping stages, over the last 20 years. Working by myself, it's hard to keep the motivation up, particularly when I've proven the concept and now have to do all the boring stuff. 

It feels more like when I was making mods with other modders back in 2007. You brainstorm ideas together, find the best ones, and have one of the other guys (AI now) go implement it. Maybe it's a work of art, maybe it's the worst code you've ever seen. Both are reasonable products of whatever AI you hand it to. 

But the key point is I now feel like more of a game designer, considering the full idea, than a solo developer trying prove single ideas in primitive ways. 

It feels collaborative in similar ways to my professional career. Some times we handed something off to a dev, and it was completely misunderstood. That's what the review process is for. AI can be the same. 

For me, it frees me up from the mundane and the stuff I just couldn't piece together myself. How to do 100k 3d animated units on screen in a Web browser? I had AI work on it with me and we made it work. I'm aiming for around 500k now since the concept is proven. 

I feel now I can turn any concept into reality as long as the tech basis is there. If I can think of it, AI can help me achieve it. It struggles to come up with ideas anywhere near as good as mine. But if I can tell it my vision, it can usually find some way to succeed. It may not be the most elegant solution. Maybe I'll code that when I understand it completely.

replies.author: ModernGameDev
replies.body: You’ve described this better than I ever could haha. I think the word “collaborative” is key. Even though AI does most of the work, we still have to put in the work ourselves to create something great.

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
It's that which will separate us from the slop accusations I feel. It feels so reminiscent of the early Asset Store days. Everything Unity was considered a worthless asset flip for a while until the good games made themselves known. 

These days using Unity is probably more recommended than Unreal given the beast it is and that "unoptimized unreal" aspect many games seem to have. For a while people hated on all Unreal Engine games too. 

The barrier to entry has been lowered. So there will be more "slop" or "this is my first game ever", but there will also be "this is my unique combination of ideas nobody had ever tried before", and *that* is what I'm most excited about.

replies.author: ModernGameDev
replies.body: Yes and that’s what I want to teach. I don’t see anyone on YouTube or any social media platform teaching how to effectively use and collaborate AI to make games that you’d actually enjoy playing

comments.author: Vindelator
comments.body:
I'm a writer by trade. Here's two conflicting thoughts. 

Whenever I talk about how I use AI for visuals, people literally tell me to stop and become a shitty visual artist who sucks at his job.

It's frustrating to have to justify my choice on that.

But on the flip side, man, I hate how AI writes. It writes like the world's most average schmuck: the milquetoast guy who never gets a second date.

I still can't draw, but I do see the value in it.

replies.author: ModernGameDev
replies.body:
Tbh idc what other people say to me about using AI because they’re not there helping make the dang thing and most of them don’t know how stressful coding can really be.

And that’s cool I’m learning how to write fiction stories because I have some game ideas that are story focused. It does repeat some of the same tropes but again it’s a context issue like anything with AI

replies.author: Vindelator
replies.body:
Yeah, I'm an old man and I don't really need people to agree with me anymore on my creative process. Not really. But it does suck if an AI visual is a non-starter for the audience. (It should only be a non-starter if it sucks!)

If you're dealing with tropes, that's not a sin. Especially for a game. So long as the sum of the parts of whatever you make is good in the end or fresh in some other ways. This is a good screenwriters resource for that but mostly it's fun reading: 

[https://tvtropes.org/](https://tvtropes.org/)

comments.author: Idem_dito
comments.body: Thank you for the write up. I have a question: how do you practically do this. How do you build a team if agents that knows how to route and doesnt burn up your tokens like madmen. I work in claude cli.

replies.author: ModernGameDev
replies.body:
I still like to be the guy in the loop. I don’t trust AI enough to run big tasks on their own yet. I use the Claude code plugin with VS code and give it small 5-10min tasks and then I look over it. Then I use separate services to generate art, create music, etc but I don’t use them all at once. I pay for a month then spend that whole month getting what I need done then canceling it to save money. But I always keep Claude code paid for.

In the future I’m going to create actual guides and YouTube tutorials(once I get a new computer, I’m very broke atm) to really explain my philosophy and process
